channel.title: Signal Brief · Policy
channel.description: Signal Brief: the day in technology, in The Signal's own words. Every item is written from linked official sources and fact checked before publication.

item.title: US midterm results put data centre building under pressure
item.description: Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the United States midterm elections on Tuesday, a result that carries direct consequences for data centre building. Voters decided 41 ballot measures about data centres across 10 states, and all but one went against data centre development, with Harwood in North Dakota the only exception. Texas, one of the largest data centre hubs, saw Democrats win races up and down the ballot, and candidates from both parties had campaigned against data centre expansion in several states. Why it matters for tech: Election results now shape where data centres can be built, turning local planning fights into a national question for the AI buildout.

item.title: OpenAI drops NDAs with public officials for its data centre projects
item.description: OpenAI published a National Community Compact and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint setting out commitments for future compute campuses it owns and operates, including paying the full cost of the electricity it uses and publishing the jobs it expects to create. It will not use non-disclosure agreements with public officials, allowing only narrow protections for security information, trade secrets or proprietary information. The announcement follows midterm votes in which US voters decided local data centre measures. Why it matters for tech: Data centre deals have drawn scrutiny over secrecy and local costs, and OpenAI is putting its community terms in writing rather than leaving them to negotiation.

item.title: US voters decide 41 local data centre measures in the midterm elections
item.description: Ballotpedia counted 41 local ballot measures on data centre policy across 10 states on November 3: 28 would limit development and 13 would facilitate it. In reported results, Edgewater, Florida voted to add a ban on new data centres to its city charter, Alhambra, California voted to prohibit data centres, and Harwood, North Dakota rejected its restrictive measure, the only one voted down in USA Today's tally of local results. Why it matters for tech: Local ballot outcomes now directly decide where large data centres can be built in the United States.

item.title: IQM calls for an EU Quantum Act with dedicated qubit foundries
item.description: In a report titled Quantum Is Europe's Second Chance, IQM Quantum Computers calls on the EU to pass a Quantum Act. It proposes dedicated qubit foundries, more late stage growth capital and DARPA style procurement, arguing that Europe is strong in public investment and deployments but weaker in venture capital, chip manufacturing and regulatory speed. Why it matters for tech: The proposal shows industry shaping the EU quantum policy agenda before legislation is drafted.

item.title: Russia plans underground data centres after Ukrainian drone strikes
item.description: Ars Technica reports that Ukrainian drone strikes on exposed Russian infrastructure have prompted Russian plans to move data centres underground. Russia's Digital Development Ministry has confirmed, as reported by Kommersant, that it completed drone protection recommendations for data centres, covering underground siting for the most critical sites, and sent them to the relevant organisations. Why it matters for tech: The conflict is directly reshaping where and how a major state builds and protects its data centre capacity.
